cards.front: The 70-kg reference man is 60 percent water, a total body water of about {{c1::42 L}}.
cards.back: A textbook convention for arithmetic, not a measurement of anyone.
cards.quote: Physiology texts use a 70-kg reference man whose body is 60 percent water: total body water (TBW) of about 42 L.

cards.front: In the 70-kg reference man, how is total body water (42 L) divided between intracellular and extracellular fluid?
cards.back: ICF about two-thirds, 28 L; ECF about one-third, 14 L.
cards.quote: Intracellular fluid (ICF), the water inside cells: about two-thirds of TBW, 28 L.

cards.front: In the 70-kg reference man, how is the 14 L of extracellular fluid divided?
cards.back: About three-quarters interstitial fluid (10.5 L), one-quarter plasma (3.5 L). Transcellular fluid is usually counted with the ECF.
cards.quote: About three-quarters of it is interstitial fluid (ISF), the fluid that bathes cells (10.5 L), and one-quarter is plasma

cards.front: About what fraction of body mass is water in infants, in old age, and in young-adult men and women on average?
cards.back: Infants about 75 percent by one textbook estimate; can fall to about 45 percent in old age; young-adult averages about 59 percent (men) and 50 percent (women), with wide ranges.
cards.quote: Infants are about 75 percent water by one textbook estimate, and the fraction can fall to about 45 percent in old age.

cards.front: Why does a person with more body fat have a lower water fraction of body mass?
cards.back: Lean tissue is roughly 73 percent water and adipose tissue far less, so more fat lowers the fraction. Women carry more fat on average.
cards.quote: lean tissue is roughly 73 percent water and adipose tissue far less, so more fat means a lower water fraction.

cards.front: Which barrier separates ICF from ECF, which separates plasma from ISF, and what solute class does each barrier divide water by?
cards.back: Cell membrane (ICF/ECF): small solutes such as sodium salts. Capillary wall (plasma/ISF): protein, mainly albumin, via oncotic pressure.
cards.why: Small solutes cross most capillaries outside the brain freely, so they do not divide plasma from ISF.
cards.quote: So the cell membrane divides water by small solutes such as sodium salts, and the capillary wall by protein.

cards.front: Sodium leaks into cells. Why does it still behave as the ECF's effective solute?
cards.back: The sodium-potassium pump moves it back out, so sodium salts act as if they could not enter cells.
cards.why: Likewise potassium leaks out but the pump returns it, so it effectively stays inside with the cell's trapped anions.
cards.quote: Sodium leaks in, but the sodium-potassium pump moves it back out, so it behaves as if it could not enter: sodium salts are the ECF's effective solute.

cards.front: State the rule that decides how body water divides between cells and extracellular fluid.
cards.back: Water crosses cell membranes until every litre holds the same concentration of effective solute, so each compartment holds water in proportion to the effective osmoles trapped in it.
cards.quote: Water crosses cell membranes until every litre of body water holds the same concentration of effective solute

cards.front: To predict where a gain or loss of water and sodium salts goes, into which two parts do you split it, and where does each part go?
cards.back: Isotonic part: stays where its solute stays (sodium salts, outside cells). Free-water part: shared by all body water in proportion to the volumes once the isotonic part is placed.
cards.quote: The isotonic part stays where its solute stays: for sodium salts, outside cells.

cards.front: Why can the effective-solute rule not tell how extracellular water splits between plasma and interstitial fluid?
cards.back: At the capillary wall small solutes are not effective. The plasma/ISF split needs Starling forces or the reference 1:3 fractions.
cards.quote: At the capillary wall small solutes are not effective at all, so this rule does not split ECF into plasma and ISF.

cards.front: A drug fully blocks the sodium-potassium pump in a cell that holds anions that cannot leave. Predict what happens to the cell's volume and why.
cards.back: The cell swells. Sodium leaking in now stays, adding particles inside; water follows.
cards.why: Rests on the pump keeping sodium effectively outside, which keeps outside as crowded as inside.
cards.quote: Without the pump, sodium leaking in would add to the particles inside, water would follow, and cells would swell.
cards.section: Why cells do not swell on their own

cards.front: Osmolality is osmoles of dissolved particles per {{c1::kilogram of water}}; osmolarity is the same count per litre of solution.
cards.back: Adult plasma osmolality is typically about 275 to 295 mOsm per kg.
cards.quote: Osmoregulation defined osmolality: osmoles of dissolved particles per kilogram of water.
cards.section: Osmolality counts particles; tonicity counts the ones that stay on one side

cards.front: What is tonicity (effective osmolality)?
cards.back: The concentration of only those solutes that cannot cross the membrane in question over the time considered; only they hold water on one side.
cards.quote: Tonicity, or effective osmolality, counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane in question over the time considered
cards.section: Osmolality counts particles; tonicity counts the ones that stay on one side

cards.front: A red cell is placed in a urea solution with the same osmolality as plasma. Why does it swell?
cards.back: Urea crosses the cell membrane, moves into the cell, and water follows. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic: urea raises osmolality, not tonicity.
cards.quote: Urea crosses the cell membrane, so it moves into the cell and water follows.
cards.section: Osmolality counts particles; tonicity counts the ones that stay on one side

cards.front: A bag of 5% dextrose is nearly isosmotic with plasma. Why does it act in the body like solute-free water?
cards.back: Once the body takes up and uses the glucose, only water remains.
cards.quote: But once the body takes up and uses the glucose, what is left behaves as solute-free water.
cards.section: Osmolality counts particles; tonicity counts the ones that stay on one side

cards.front: 5% dextrose holds 50 g of dextrose monohydrate (molar mass about 198) per litre. Estimate its osmolarity.
cards.back: 50 / 198 = 0.252 mol per L, about 252 mOsm per L, a little below plasma.
cards.quote: so the label gives about 252 mOsm per L (50 ÷ 198), a little below plasma.
cards.section: Osmolality counts particles; tonicity counts the ones that stay on one side

cards.front: Closed reference model (ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, both 300 mOsm per kg; no excretion; cells gain or lose no solute). A man retains 2 L of isotonic saline. Give final osmolality, ICF and ECF.
cards.back: Adds 600 mOsm and 2 L outside cells. C = 13,200 / 44 = 300, unchanged. ICF = 8,400 / 300 = 28 L (no change); ECF = 16 L (+2 L).
cards.why: Nothing made the compartments unequally concentrated, so no water crossed cell membranes.
cards.quote: Nothing made the rooms unequally crowded, so no water crossed a cell membrane.
cards.section: Where does the litre go? Three trials

cards.front: Closed reference model (ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, 300 mOsm per kg, plasma sodium 140 mmol per L). A man retains 1 L of solute-free water. Predict final osmolality, ICF, ECF and plasma sodium.
cards.back: C = 12,600 / 43 = 293. ICF 28.67 L (+0.67), ECF 14.33 L (+0.33). Plasma sodium = 140 × 42/43, about 136.7 mmol per L, with no sodium lost.
cards.why: No solute added, so the litre is shared in proportion to existing water, 28 of 42 parts to cells.
cards.quote: Plasma sodium is diluted in the same proportion, 140 × 42 / 43, to about 136.7 mmol per L.
cards.section: Where does the litre go? Three trials

cards.front: Closed reference model (ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, both 300 mOsm per kg; added NaCl stays outside cells). A man retains 1 L of NaCl at 600 mOsm per L. Find final osmolality, ICF and ECF.
cards.why: The salt raises outside crowding, so water leaves cells until concentrations match.
cards.quote: The salt made the outside room more crowded, and water left the cells until the crowding matched.
cards.section: Where does the litre go? Three trials

cards.front: In the closed reference model (ECF 14 L, plasma one-quarter of ECF), how much plasma volume does 1 L of retained isotonic saline add, and how much does 1 L of retained solute-free water add?
cards.back: Saline: 0.25 L to plasma (0.75 L to ISF). Water: one-third of a litre to ECF, a quarter of that to plasma, about 0.08 L.
cards.quote: With plasma taken as one-quarter of the ECF, Trial A puts 0.25 L in plasma and 0.75 L in ISF, and Trial B puts only about 0.08 L in plasma.
cards.section: A shortcut: split any load into isotonic saline and water

cards.front: In hyponatremia from water retention, plasma sodium falls. What has changed, and what has not?
cards.back: The ratio of cation to water fell; total body sodium did not. Low plasma sodium means too much water for the cation present.
cards.quote: Body sodium did not fall; the ratio of cation to water did
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: Why is acute severe hyponatremia dangerous, and why can a fast rise in plasma sodium harm brain cells after they have adapted?
cards.back: Brain cells swell inside a rigid skull (cerebral edema). Over hours to days they shed potassium, chloride and organic osmolytes; a fast sodium rise then shrinks them.
cards.quote: That is why, once they have adapted, a fast rise in plasma sodium can shrink them.
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: Closed reference model (ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, 300 mOsm per kg, plasma sodium 140 mmol per L). As bookkeeping, 300 mOsm of effective solute (potassium salt) leaves the cells and the body; nothing else changes. Find ICF, ECF and plasma sodium.
cards.back: C = 12,300 / 42 = 292.9. ICF = 8,100 / 292.9 = 27.66 L; ECF = 14.34 L. Plasma sodium = 140 × 14 / 14.34, about 136.7 mmol per L, with no sodium lost.
cards.quote: Potassium salts are the cells' stuck guests.
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: Plasma sodium concentration tracks what body quantity?
cards.back: All exchangeable cation, sodium plus potassium, per litre of body water; not the body's sodium stock.
cards.quote: So plasma sodium tracks all the exchangeable cation, sodium and potassium, per litre of body water.
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: In 98 chronically ill patients (most with all three measured), exchangeable sodium, exchangeable potassium and total body water were measured by isotope dilution and compared with serum sodium. What was found, what does it support, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Serum sodium correlated poorly with any single store and closely with (Na_e + K_e) / TBW. Supports passive water distribution by osmotically active solute, cell potassium counting like ECF sodium. Limits: correlation in sick patients, not intervention; exchangeable is not total cation.
cards.quote: serum sodium correlated poorly with any single store, and closely with exchangeable sodium plus potassium per litre of body water.
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: An edematous patient has excess total body sodium yet a low plasma sodium. How can both be true?
cards.back: Plasma sodium reports exchangeable sodium plus potassium per litre of body water. If water is retained in greater proportion than cation, the ratio falls even though the sodium stock is high.
cards.quote: Edematous patients with excess body sodium could be hyponatremic.
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: A patient has low plasma sodium from potassium depletion, with normal body sodium and water. Using the closed-model rule, predict the effect of restoring cell potassium (with its anion) on plasma sodium, and why.
cards.back: Plasma sodium rises. Restored potassium salts are effective solute inside cells, so cells draw water back from the ECF, concentrating ECF sodium.
cards.why: Rests on plasma sodium tracking sodium plus potassium per litre of body water.
cards.quote: Fewer of them, and cells hold less water; that water moves out and dilutes the ECF.
cards.section: Plasma sodium reports water, not body sodium

cards.front: Plasma: sodium 145 mmol per L, glucose 108 mg/dL, BUN 28 mg/dL. Estimate osmolality and tonicity.
cards.back: Osmolality = 2 × 145 + 108/18 + 28/2.8 = 290 + 6 + 10 = 306 mOsm per kg. Tonicity leaves out urea: 290 + 6 = 296 mOsm per kg.
cards.quote: Estimated tonicity leaves urea out: 2[Na+] + glucose / 18, so for the example above, 280 + 5 = 285 mOsm per kg.

cards.front: In estimating tonicity from lab values, why is urea left out but glucose kept?
cards.back: Urea crosses most cell membranes and equilibrates. Glucose enters many cells, such as muscle, only slowly, more slowly when insulin action is low.
cards.quote: Urea is dropped because it crosses most cell membranes and equilibrates.

cards.front: A patient has sodium 140 mmol per L, glucose 90 mg/dL and BUN 140 mg/dL. Calculate estimated osmolality and tonicity, and predict whether the high BUN shrinks cells.
cards.back: Osmolality = 280 + 5 + 50 = 335 mOsm per kg; tonicity = 280 + 5 = 285, normal. Cells are not expected to shrink.
cards.why: Urea crosses most cell membranes, so it raises osmolality but not tonicity.
cards.quote: Urea raises osmolality but not tonicity.
cards.section: Osmolality counts particles; tonicity counts the ones that stay on one side

cards.front: A man bleeds quickly. In the first minutes, does his plasma sodium change, and does water leave his cells? What happens later across the capillary wall?
cards.back: Neither changes at first: hemorrhage removes isotonic whole blood. Later, as capillary pressure falls, ISF moves into plasma over minutes to hours, so hematocrit falls.
cards.quote: So plasma sodium does not change at first, and there is no net water shift across cell membranes.
cards.section: Losses: bleeding and pure water loss

cards.front: Closed reference model (ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, 300 mOsm per kg, plasma sodium 140 mmol per L). A man loses 3 L of pure water. Find osmolality, ICF, ECF and plasma sodium.
cards.why: Pure water loss is all free-water part, shared by all body water, two-thirds from cells.
cards.quote: Pure water loss, such as water lost in breath, is all free-water part.
cards.section: Losses: bleeding and pure water loss

cards.front: By indicator dilution, how is a compartment volume calculated, and what must the marker do?
cards.back: V = (amount given − amount lost) / (mixed concentration − baseline). The marker must mix evenly through its space and no further, not be metabolized, and its urinary loss be measured.
cards.quote: This assumes the marker mixes evenly through its space and no further, is not metabolized, and its urinary loss is measured.

cards.front: Which marker measures total body water, which measures ECF, and which measures plasma volume?
cards.back: TBW: heavy water (deuterium oxide). ECF: inulin or bromide. Plasma: Evans blue (binds albumin) or labelled albumin.
cards.quote: Heavy water (deuterium oxide) crosses capillary walls and cell membranes: TBW.

cards.front: How are ICF and ISF volumes obtained, and why are they the least certain?
cards.back: By subtraction: ICF = TBW − ECF; ISF = ECF − plasma. They have no marker of their own, so errors in both measurements end up in the difference.
cards.quote: ICF and ISF have no marker of their own, so they come by subtraction

cards.front: What two routine corrections are applied to heavy-water and albumin-marker measurements, and why?
cards.back: Heavy-water space is divided by about 1.04 because deuterium exchanges with hydrogen on non-water molecules. Albumin-marker concentrations are extrapolated back to injection time because the marker leaks slowly out of plasma.
cards.quote: Albumin markers leak slowly out of plasma, so samples taken after mixing are extrapolated back to the time of injection.

cards.front: An adult receives 2.0 g inulin (0.2 g in urine by sampling; plasma 0.12 g per L, baseline zero) and 12 mg Evans blue (extrapolated plasma 4.0 mg per L). Raw heavy-water space is 41.6 L (exchange factor 1.04). Find ECF, plasma, TBW, ICF and ISF.
cards.quote: Forget the inulin in urine and ECF comes out 15.0 L.

cards.front: In a crossover study, healthy men received 2 L of 0.9% saline or 2 L of 5% dextrose over one hour. What did the timing of excretion show about the static compartment model?
cards.back: All dextrose water was excreted within two hours; only about one-third of the saline by six hours. The model says where a load goes; the kidney sets how long it stays.
cards.quote: all the dextrose water had been excreted by two hours after the infusion ended, but only about one-third of the saline's sodium and water by six hours.

cards.front: Volunteers retain 1 L of isotonic saline. If ECF divides by reference volumes (plasma 3.5 L, one-quarter), what plasma volume and albumin dilution are predicted at equilibrium, and how would you read a larger plasma gain?
cards.back: Plasma 3.5 to 3.75 L, about 7 percent albumin dilution if albumin stays in plasma. A larger gain may mean distribution is still under way or vessels and tissues are not filling in proportion; the time course and bromide space separate these.
cards.quote: A plasma gain near one-quarter of the retained volume supports the model.

cards.front: With nothing excreted and plasma one-quarter of a 14 L ECF (3.5 L), what fall in albumin concentration does the model predict after 2 L of isotonic saline? About 20 percent was seen; give two explanations.
cards.back: Plasma 3.5 to 4.0 L; albumin × 3.5/4.0 = 0.875, a 12.5 percent fall. A 20 percent fall could mean the load had not yet left plasma, or albumin itself left.
cards.quote: For Lobo's 2 L, with nothing excreted, the model predicts a 12.5 percent fall (3.5/4.0)

cards.front: A patient with edema has ICF 28 L and an expanded ECF of 22 L. In the closed model, how much of 1 L of retained solute-free water enters cells? Is it still two-thirds?
cards.back: 28/50 of a litre, 0.56 L, not two-thirds. Free water is shared in proportion to the water already in each compartment.
cards.why: Two-thirds is the cells' share in the reference man (28 of 42), not a constant of the body.
cards.quote: In a person whose ECF is expanded (edema) or whose cell mass is small, the share differs.

cards.front: Each osmole per kilogram lowers the freezing point of water about 1.86 degrees C. Estimate the freezing point of a sample at 300 mOsm per kg.
cards.quote: Each osmole per kilogram lowers the freezing point about 1.86 degrees C

cards.front: Measured plasma osmolality is 320 mOsm per kg; the estimate from sodium, glucose and BUN is 290. Interpret.
cards.back: Osmolal gap = 320 − 290 = 30 mOsm per kg, a wide gap pointing to an unmeasured solute such as an alcohol.
cards.quote: a wide gap points to an unmeasured solute, such as an alcohol (not the anion gap of acid-base balance).
